Registered Office: Charles House, 108-110 Finchley Road, London NW3 5JJ June 2012 Vol 39 No 12 ### By-product revenues from gold, silver and molybdenum Most copper ore bodies also contain other metals, principally gold, silver, platinum group metals (pgms) or molybdenum, which can be recovered alongside the copper. Gold and silver are recovered into the copper concentrates, while molybdenum is recovered into a separate concentrate. Other by-products include lead, zinc, nickel and cobalt which may also be recovered into separate concentrates. If the precious metals contained in the copper concentrates are above a threshold level, the miner will be paid and the revenues from these by-products may provide significant additional revenue. Gold and silver prices rose to record levels in 2011, as global economic uncertainty increased their attractiveness to investors, and as a result miners saw their by-product revenues increase significantly, offsetting the impact of rising input costs. In this article we examine recent trends in total by-product revenues and compare revenues across regions. We then focus in on gold, silver and molybdenum and identify the main producers of these byproducts, and discuss the impact of by-product revenues on total revenues and net of by-product costs.  2012 CRU International Limited confidential www.cruonline.crugroup.com

p.com COPPER STUDIES June 2012 2 ### By-product revenues for main product copper mines Introduction Many main product copper mines are able to recover by-products from the processing of copper containing ores, thereby earning additional revenue. The main by-products are gold and silver, but a number of miners in North and South America and Asia also recover molybdenum, while some of the mines in the African copperbelt also produce cobalt. Copper is also mined with lead and zinc in other parts of the world, particularly Peru, Canada and Australia. The miners receive revenues from the gold and silver contained in concentrates, while in the case of molybdenum and other the metals a separate concentrate or refined metal is produced. In this article we look at recent trends in by-product revenues and the impact on net costs, both over time and across regions. We then look in more detail at prices and by-product output of gold silver and molybdenum, highlighting the key producers. The analysis focuses mostly on main product copper mines. ### Recent trends: high by-product revenues offset the impact of rising operating costs Over the last five years mine operating costs have generally been on an upward trend. Although they declined year-on-year in 2009 due to the onset of the global recession, they have subsequently regained their upward momentum. However by-product revenues have shown a similar trend, after declining in 2008 and 2009 they have risen strongly over the last 3 years, offsetting much of the increase in operating costs. As a result, net of by-product costs (NoBP) have risen only mildly over the period, with the exception of a blip in 2008 when operating costs rose steeply before the recession hit. Data from CRU’s copper mine cost model shows that while operating costs rose by 44% between 2006 and 2011, byproduct revenues were up by 51% with the result that NoBP costs only increased by 39%, and between 2008 and 2011 they were only up by 1% compared to a rise in operating costs of 14%. Gold and silver prices have risen steadily over the last 10 years, only pausing for breath in late 2008/early 2009 before increasing even more steeply over the last 3 years. Gold, in particular, has benefited from its “safe haven” status in times of financial uncertainty, and silver has piggy-backed on gold. Molybdenum prices, on the other hand, have struggled to recover from a sharp fall in the second half of 2009. Increased capacity coincided with a slump in demand and any subsequent growth in demand has been more than offset by additions to mine output. ### Chile benefits least from by-product revenues There

is considerable diversity in by-product revenues across regions, with implications for the mines’ relative NoBP costs and competitive positions. Mines in Chile have the lowest by-product revenues, and as a consequence have high NoBP costs, despite having the lowest operating costs. Major mines in the region have relatively low contents of payable precious metals, although several of Codelco’s mines produce significant tonnages of molybdenum, which is also produced at Los Pelambres, Los Bronces and Collahuasi. Mines in neighbouring Peru have similar operating costs, but higher by-product revenues and considerably lower NoBP costs. Revenues are boosted by higher gold and silver values in the concentrates, while major mines Antamina, Cerro Verde, Cuajone and Toquepala all also produce molybdenum, and Antamina also benefits from zinc. In contrast, Australia has the second highest operating costs but due to high by-product revenues it has the lowest NoBP costs - which are actually negative. It has a number of mines which produce concentrates with high gold values, including Newcrest’s Cadia and Telfer operations and Newmont’s Boddington. For these three mines the value of the gold in the concentrates is higher than the copper, and they should be considered as gold mines with by-product copper. Canada, with its polymetallic mines is the region with the second highest by-product revenues, but the high operating costs means that it still ranks top for NoBP costs. A number of mines in the region have high silver or gold values in the concentrates. By product revenues

Ranking fourth in terms of operating costs, Asia has the second lowest NoBP costs, while Europe’s ranking drops from third highest to fourth highest once by-products are taken into account. A number of Asian mines have high gold values, including Freeport McMoRan’s Grasberg and Newmont’s Batu Hijau operations in Indonesia and Philex’s Padcal in the Philippines, while Kazakhmys’ mines have high silver values. In Europe, Boliden’s Aitik has by-product gold and silver and KGHM’s mines are very high in silver. ### Gold and silver prices maintain upward trend Gold and silver prices have risen steadily over the last 10 years, with growth particularly marked during the global recession of the last 3 years. The prices for both metals declined in the second half of 2008, temporarily halting the long term upward trend, but then quickly recovered; the gold price gained former levels in Q1 of 2009 while silver had recovered by the end of 2009. Since then, the gold price has been driven by speculative demand and reached an all time high of $1,886/oz in August 2011. It has benef

ited from its “safe haven” status in times of economic uncertainty with investors moving funds into gold from other more risky assets. Silver normally attracts less speculative investment than gold since it is more of an industrial metal, but nevertheless the price has moved up in the wake of the gold price. Indeed during 2011 it rose more steeply than gold. During the ten year period from 2001 to 2011 the gold price increased nearly six fold, while silver went up by a multiple of 8, increasing by 74% in 2011 alone. As a result, miners enjoyed a substantial increase in by-product revenues. Both prices have been volatile, however, responding to the variability of economic news emerging from Europe, the USA and China. Going forward, we see the economic instability continuing to affect prices, but despite the high volatility witnessed over the past few months, we expect gold to keep its safe haven investment status. Nevertheless, there will be long periods of market consolidation as investors liquidate their positions to cover margin calls, causing large and Miners benefit from steep rise in gold and silver prices

In 2013, we expect global economic conditions to start improving and interest rates to begin rising. This will put pressure on gold prices and eventually halt the price rally, as investors’ appetite for risk improves. After 2012, we foresee the average gold price sliding from its 2012 peak level. As silver shares some of the safe haven credentials of gold it is expected to follow the general trend in the gold price. However, as silver is also suitable for industrial use, the dim economic outlook is expected to lead to a relatively sharper drop in prices and a widening gold-silver price ratio in the coming years. ### Revenues from by-product gold and silver Precious metals are the main source of byproduct revenues for copper miners. Due to its high value, gold has the potential to provide the greater revenue, but fewer mines have payable gold in their concentrates than silver. Miners are paid for the gold and silver that are present in the copper concentrates which can be recovered into metal by smelters and refiners, either into refined metal or in residues that can be sold on for refining. For gold, typically 1g/t is “free” to the smelters while for silver 1530g/t is not paid for. For concentrates with exceptionally high gold or silver contents the payable level is 95%, while smelters in the Far East pay for the precious metals contents according to a sliding scale as indicated in the table. In addition a refining charge is deducted from the payment, typically $5/oz for gold and 35¢/oz for silver. Some mines which have a high gold content in the ore also recover gold into a separate dorй via gravity separation. This is then sold to a precious metal refiner. The tables on the following pages list the copper mines with significant by-product gold and/or silver in their concentrates. Australasia and South East Asia are the main regions for mines with high gold production, although there are a smattering of mines in South and North America and Europe. However, as already noted above, the top 3 mines, Boddington, Telfer and Cadia are really main product gold mines producing significant amounts of by-product copper. Silver shows a different regional distribution; the top mines are located in Europe, with North America and central Asia (Kazakhstan, Turkey) also prevalent. Again there are a few mines in South America and also Australasia. The mines are ordered according to the gold or silver content of the concentrates expressed in terms of grammes per tonne. The regional distribution of average gold and silver grades is also illustrated in the chart below and helps to explain the regional disparity in by-product revenues noted above. Australasia, which has the highest by-product revenues, also has the highest average grade of gold in concentrates. The impact of this far outweighs the relatively low average silver grades due to the much greater value of gold. Neighbouring Peru ranks fourth for both gold and silver, explaining its higher average by-product revenues. Europe tops the ranking for silver with KGHM’s and Boliden’s mines having high silver values, while North America ranks second for

both gold and silver. The gold grades of concentrates are much lower than the silver grades reflecting the lower grade of the ore. However, with the gold around 50 times more valuable than silver, the potential revenues are considerably higher. A simple calculation illustrates the relative values of the two metals contained in concentrates. For mines with payable gold the weighted average gold content of concentrates is 12g/t. After deducting 1g/t, this is worth $586/t of concentrates at the current gold price of $1,600/oz ($51.4/g). For a concentrate grading 27% copper, this would be $2,170 per tonne of copper. The weighted average silver content of concentrates is 152g/t. After deducting 30g/t this is worth $129/t of concentrates at the current silver price of $33/oz and $478/t of copper for a 27% concentrate. Molybdenum: price still suffering from over supply
In common with all metals, molybdenum prices fell sharply at the end of 2008 with the onset of the
global recession. However, unlike copper, which quickly recovered back to pre-recession levels, the
molybdenum price has struggled to make significant gains. In the first half of the last decade prices
spiked at an unprecedented - and unsustainable - level of $36/lb due to a shortage of roasting capacity for
processing concentrates into oxide which resulted in a tight market for oxide. Towards the end of the
decade this shortfall had been overcome but the industry then faced a slump in demand as the recession
impacted steel demand, which accounts for some two-thirds of molybdenum consumption.

Demand is currently reported to be stable, supported by robust demand for steel from the motor vehicles and energy sectors and a solid performance from the food processing industry in Europe. Demand is also solid from the construction industry. However surplus supply continues to weigh on prices. CRU expects that this situation of oversupply will persist, preventing any significant improvement in the price beyond the $14-15/lb range. With a number of copper projects in the pipeline that will produce byproduct molybdenum, opportunities for higher prices in the future

are also limited. ### Molybdenum revenues Molybdenum ranks second in importance as a by-product of copper production, and is mostly produced in North and South America and Asia. Mines with significant production are shown in the table below. Molybdenum is recovered into a separate molybdenum concentrate. During flotation, a copper/molybdenum concentrate is recovered which is then further processed to separate the molybdenum from the copper. The molybdenum concentrate is leached to remove residual copper and roasted to produce molybdenum oxide. Most by-product producers sell unleached concentrate, but Freeport McMoRan has its own processing facilities at Sierrita in the USA while there is also a molybdenum roaster at Collahuasi that processes concentrates from Collahuasi and other Chilean miners. Chilean concentrates are also treated by Molymet at its plant at Nos near Santiago. Production of by-product molybdenum is dominated by Codelco (Chile), Freeport McMoRan (USA and Peru) and Grupo Mexico (Mexico and Peru). Codelco recovers molybdenum concentrates at all of its copper concentrate operations, with production totalling 23,000t, 51Mlbs in 2011. Freeport McMoRan recovers molybdenum at its Sierrita, Morenci and Bagdad concentrate mines in the USA and Cerro Verde in Peru. It also operates main product molybdenum mines and processing facilities in the USA. Other significant producers include Rio Tinto subsidiary Kennecott Utah Copper at Bingham Canyon, Highland Valley, Antamina, Collahuasi and Los Pelambres. The Bingham Canyon mine is the largest by-product producer, with output of 13,600t (30Mlbs) in 2011. Asian producers of by-product molybdenum include NICICO, Jiangxi Copper at Dexing and Erdenet in Mongolia. Of significance for revenues, however, is not the total production but the ratio of molybdenum to copper output. This is indicated in the final column of the table which shows molybdenum output as a percentage of copper output. A regional comparison indicating actual molybdenum output per tonne of copper output is shown in the chart below. Molybdenum to copper production ratios and hence revenues per tonne of copper are highest in the USA and Mexico, with Mercator Minerals having the highest value at its Mineral Park operation. The final chart illustrates the impact on revenues. With a high molybdenum to copper production ratio at Mineral Park, molybdenum revenues (before processing charges) for Mercator Minerals totalled some $6,000/t of copper produced in 2011, more than two-thirds of the value of the copper. For all producers revenues from molybdenum provided a useful boost to overall income, although for the majority of miners the revenues were below $1,000/t of copper, with the lowest at Los Bronces at just $180/t. ### Company revenues A small number of producers are able to benefit from revenues from all three products discussed above, and many earn revenues from two. A number of mines have both payable gold and payable silver, while most of the producers of by-product molybdenum also have by-product gold or silver, mostly silver. Indeed, Bingham Canyon (KUC) has all three. The chart below illustrates the importance of by-product revenues to total income for some key producers. The figures are based on gross mine revenues or sales figures as reported by the companies. For the top four producers of by-product precious metals and molybdenum, by-products account for as much as one-third of total revenues. For Freeport Indonesia (Grasberg) and Ok Tedi this is from gold, but Mercator and Kennecott (KUC) also earn significant revenues from molybdenum. Such high by-product revenues significantly reduce the NoBP costs for these producers with positive implications for their competitive position and their
